opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that a lot of what's scientifically interesting about it comes precisely *from* the uncertainty. I've been something of a professional skeptic about quantum machine learning for years. I wrote a piece called "Read the Fine Print" because so many of the claimed exponential speedups came with caveats buried in the assumptions. You need some magical way to load your classical data into a quantum state, or you only get a quantum state as output when what you wanted was the actual answer, or the matrix has to be sparse and well-conditioned in just the right way.

What happened next is, to me, a beautiful example of how theoretical computer science is supposed to work. Ewin Tang, as an undergraduate, took the quantum recommendation systems algorithm of Kerenidis and Prakash, which had been one of the best candidates for an exponential speedup on a practical machine learning problem, and showed you could "dequantize" it. If you give the classical algorithm the same kind of sampling access you implicitly gave the quantum one, you get a classical algorithm that's only polynomially slower. That opened up a whole research program of asking, for each proposed quantum speedup, whether the advantage comes from quantum mechanics or from the input model.

So even if quantum machine learning never beats a GPU cluster on some commercially relevant task, which is entirely possible, it's forced us to sharpen our understanding of where quantum advantage really comes from. Is it interference? Entanglement? The ability to sample from distributions that are hard to sample from classically? Those are deep questions about the boundary between classical and quantum computation, and ML has turned out to be a very productive testing ground for them.

There's also the other direction, using classical machine learning to understand quantum systems. There's nice work on learning properties of quantum states from relatively few measurements: shadow tomography, classical shadows, and so on. Some of my own work fed into that. There you get provable separations, for example in the number of experiments you need with versus without quantum memory. That's a setting where you can actually prove something, rather than just hoping a variational circuit trains well.

And then I'd separate all of that from the hype. A lot of the near-term variational stuff has the flavor of "throw a parameterized quantum circuit at the problem and see what happens." It runs into barren plateaus, and it's hard to know whether you'd have done just as well classically. I'm not saying nobody should work on it, but I'd want people to be clear-eyed about what's been shown and what hasn't.

So, to sum up: what interests me isn't the promise that quantum ML will revolutionize industry. It's that trying to make it work, and watching where it fails, keeps teaching us something fundamental about computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I've been one of the people throwing cold water on a lot of the quantum machine learning hype, so it might seem strange for me to then turn around and say the field is interesting. But I actually think both things are true, and the reason they're both true is sort of the heart of the matter.

The thing that originally got people excited, around 2008 or so, was the HHL algorithm, Harrow, Hassidim, and Lloyd, which showed that in some sense a quantum computer can solve a huge system of linear equations exponentially faster than a classical computer. And since linear algebra is the engine underneath basically all of machine learning, people immediately said, okay, exponential speedups for machine learning. And I wrote a piece years ago that I called "Read the Fine Print," because the fine print turns out to be where everything lives. You need the data to be loaded into a quantum state, which is hard. You need the matrix to be well-conditioned. And at the end you don't get the solution vector written out, you get a quantum state that encodes it, and you can only extract a few bits of information about it. Every one of those caveats is a place where the advantage can evaporate.

So why is that interesting rather than just disappointing? Because it forces the question that I think is actually the deep one: where does the power of quantum computers come from, and what kinds of problems can it attach to? We've known for thirty years that it attaches to factoring, because of Shor, and to simulating quantum systems, because that's what nature is doing anyway. Machine learning is a totally different animal. The problems are data-driven, they're statistical, they're often not even well-posed as math problems. And asking whether quantum mechanics helps there is a way of probing the boundary of what quantum computation is for.

And then there's the dequantization story, which I find genuinely beautiful. Ewin Tang, who was my undergraduate student at UT Austin, was given the task of proving that a quantum recommendation systems algorithm couldn't be matched classically. And instead she found that it could. She showed that if you give a classical algorithm the same kind of access to the data that the quantum algorithm was assuming, basically the ability to sample from the entries, then the classical algorithm can do just as well, up to polynomial factors. And that result has since spread like wildfire. A whole swath of claimed quantum machine learning speedups turned out to be artifacts of an unfair comparison.

Now, you could read that as the field eating itself. I read it as the field doing exactly what science is supposed to do. We learned something real about classical algorithms that nobody knew before. We learned that sampling access is a surprisingly powerful resource, and that a lot of what looked quantum was really just linear algebra with a particular input model. That's a discovery, even though it's a negative one from the standpoint of anyone who wanted a product.

I'll also say there's a smaller set of results that have survived the scrutiny, things where the quantum advantage comes from a genuine structure in the problem, like periodicity hiding inside the data, or where you're learning about quantum systems themselves, so the data is already quantum and there's no loading problem. Those are the places where I think there could be something real. They're much narrower than the original pitch, but narrow and real beats broad and imaginary.

So I guess my honest answer is that I find quantum machine learning interesting as an intellectual laboratory, a place where you can test what the speedup really depends on, and sometimes get surprised, including in the direction of learning that classical computers are more powerful than we thought. Whether any of it ends up on a GPU's competitor in the data center, that's a separate question, and I'd put the burden of proof firmly on the people claiming yes.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the scientific interest is that it forces us to ask very precisely what a quantum computer can contribute to learning. Where could a speedup come from? What assumptions do you need about how the data is supplied? And could a classical algorithm achieve the same thing once you give it comparable access to that data?

For example, you might have a quantum algorithm that manipulates an enormous vector very efficiently. But if loading your data into the quantum state takes an enormous amount of time, or extracting the answer does, then you haven’t necessarily gained anything. Understanding those issues is part of the science, rather than just an obstacle to doing the science.

And sometimes investigating a proposed quantum advantage leads people to discover better classical algorithms. That’s a valuable outcome! We’ve learned something about the computational structure of the problem, even if the quantum advantage disappears.

I’m especially interested in cases where the data itself comes from a quantum system. There, you don’t have to invent a reason for quantum states to enter the picture. So I think there are very interesting questions here, quite independently of whether quantum computers will help train the next generation of large language models.

sol-6.1.text:
What interests me is that it forces us to ask some very basic questions about where a quantum speedup could actually come from. You know, it’s easy to say, “A quantum state involves exponentially many amplitudes, so let’s use those to do machine learning.” The difficulty is that you don’t get to read out all those amplitudes. You have to explain how you prepare the state, what computation you perform, and how the measurement gives you something useful.

Once you account for all of that, is there still an advantage over the best classical algorithm? Sometimes a proposed quantum algorithm inspires a better classical algorithm, and the apparent advantage disappears. I regard that as scientific progress too: we’ve learned something about the structure of the problem.

And there’s a particularly natural case where the data itself is quantum—where you’re trying to learn about a quantum system. Then you don’t first have to justify encoding a giant classical dataset into a quantum state. So I’m interested in figuring out the boundaries: which learning tasks really exploit quantum mechanics, and which merely look as though they do? That’s a worthwhile question even before we know whether it will lead to a commercially useful application.
